The '''Heyde theorem''' is one of the well-known characterization theorems in [[mathematical statistics]]. According to the classical [[Kac–Bernstein theorem]], if the sum and the difference of independent random variables are independent, then these random variables have Gaussian distributions (i.e., are [[normal distribution|normally distributed]]). A generalization of this statement is the [[Darmois-Skitovich|Skitovich–Darmois theorem]], in which linear forms of <math>n</math> independent random variables are considered instead of the sum and the difference. In Heyde's theorem, the Gaussian distribution is characterized by the symmetry of the [[conditional distribution]] of one [[linear form]] given another. The theorem was proved in 1970 by [[Chris Heyde|C. C. Heyde]]<ref>{{cite journal
 | last=Heyde
 | first=C. C.
 | title=Characterization of the Normal Law by the Symmetry of a Certain Conditional Distribution
 | journal=Sankhyā: The Indian Journal of Statistics, Series A
 | volume=32
 | issue=1
 | date=March 1970
 | pages=115–118
 | jstor=25049642
}}</ref>; see also  <ref>{{cite book
 | last1=Kagan
 | first1=A. M.
 | last2=Linnik
 | first2=Yu. V.
 | last3=Rao
 | first3=C. R.
 | title=Characterization Problems of Mathematical Statistics
 | publisher=Wiley
 | location=New York
 | year=1973
 | isbn=9780471454212
}}</ref>.  

== Statement of the theorem ==
Let <math>\xi_j, j = 1, 2, \ldots, n, </math>&nbsp; be   independent random variables, and let <math>\alpha_j, \beta_j</math>&nbsp; be nonzero constants such that <math>\beta_i \alpha_i^{-1}+\beta_j \alpha_j^{-1} \ne 0</math>  for all <math>i \ne j</math>. If the conditional distribution of the linear form <math>L_2 = \beta_1\xi_1 + \cdots + \beta_n\xi_n</math> given <math>L_1 = \alpha_1\xi_1 + \cdots + \alpha_n\xi_n</math> is symmetric, then all random variables <math>\xi_j</math> have  Gaussian distributions.

The proof of the theorem relies on [[Cramér's decomposition theorem|Cramér's decomposition theorem]] for the Gaussian distribution, as well as on the following theorem of [[Józef Marcinkiewicz|Marcinkiewicz]]: if, in a neighborhood of zero, the logarithm of the characteristic function of a distribution is a polynomial, then the distribution is Gaussian.

==Generalizations to locally compact Abelian groups==

Numerous works have been devoted to generalizing Heyde's theorem to the case where independent random variables take values in a [[Locally compact abelian group|locally compact Abelian group]] and the coefficients of the linear forms are topological automorphisms of the group. A survey of these results can be found in <ref>{{cite book
 | last=Feldman
 | first=G.
 | title=Characterization of Probability Distributions on Locally Compact Abelian Groups
 | series=Mathematical Surveys and Monographs
 | volume=273
 | publisher=American Mathematical Society
 | location=Providence, RI
 | year=2023
 | isbn=978-1-4704-7295-5
}}</ref>. As an example, one of the group analogues of Heyde's theorem is given below.

'''Theorem'''<ref>{{cite journal
 | last=Feldman
 | first=G. M.
 | title=On a characterization theorem for locally compact abelian groups
 | journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields
 | volume=133
 | year=2005
 | pages=345–357
 | doi=10.1007/s00440-005-0429-4
}}</ref>. Let <math>X</math> be a second countable  locally compact Abelian group        containing no elements of order 2. Let <math>\mathrm{Aut}(X)</math> denote the group of topological automorphisms of <math>X</math>, and  let <math>\xi_j, j = 1, 2, \dots, n,</math> be independent random variables taking values in <math>X</math> with distributions <math>\mu_j</math> whose characteristic functions do not vanish. Let <math>\alpha_j, \beta_j \in \mathrm{Aut}(X)</math> and assume that <math>\beta_i \alpha_i^{-1} \pm \beta_j \alpha_j^{-1} \in \mathrm{Aut}(X)</math> for all <math>i \ne j</math>. If the conditional distribution of the linear form <math>L_2 = \beta_1 \xi_1 + \dots + \beta_n \xi_n</math> given <math>L_1 = \alpha_1 \xi_1 + \dots + \alpha_n \xi_n</math> is symmetric, then all distributions  <math>\mu_j</math> are [[Gaussian distribution on a locally compact Abelian group|Gaussian]].

The proof relies on group analogues of   Cramér's decomposition theorem  for the Gaussian distribution and the Marcinkiewicz theorem.
